description: We are MARS-SAFE Explorers, developing an AI-powered Mars habitat survival simulation. Our project monitors oxygen, water, food, power, and temperature, predicts resource shortages, and recommends emergency recovery actions. Built with React, Node.js, and Ollama AI, MARS-SAFE aims to support astronaut training and mission safety. We welcome collaborators interested in space exploration, AI, electronics, software development, and NASA data.
summary:
I started MARS-SAFE Explorers with a simple question: What happens if something goes wrong while astronauts are living on Mars?

On Earth, help is usually nearby. But on Mars, astronauts would need to handle many emergencies on their own. Even something like an oxygen leak, water shortage, or power failure could become a serious problem.

I wanted to explore how technology could help them respond to these situations.

So, I built MARS-SAFE Explorers, a simulation that monitors important resources like oxygen, water, food, and power. It allows users to experience different emergencies, see how resource levels change, and take recovery actions.

I also added AI recommendations, resource forecasting, and an ESP32 connected to an OLED display and buzzer to demonstrate real-time emergency alerts.

This is still an early prototype, but my goal is to show how AI, software, and electronics could work together to help astronauts make better decisions and stay safer during future Mars missions.
details:
MARS-SAFE Explorers — A Smarter Way to Prepare for Emergencies on Mars

The Idea Behind My Project

When I started thinking about astronauts living on Mars, one question kept coming to my mind: What would happen if something suddenly went wrong?

On Earth, we have access to emergency services and technical support. But astronauts on Mars would face a very different situation. A shortage of oxygen, a water leak, or a power failure could put their safety at risk.

I wanted to explore whether AI and electronics could help astronauts recognize these problems early and make better decisions.

What I Built

I developed MARS-SAFE Explorers, an interactive Mars survival monitoring and emergency response simulation.

The dashboard monitors essential resources, including oxygen, water, food, and power, along with habitat temperature.

Users can simulate emergencies such as oxygen leakage, water shortages, power failures, food shortages, and dangerous temperature increases.

When an emergency occurs, the system updates the resource levels, displays warnings, and allows users to activate recovery actions.

How AI Helps

I integrated a local AI model using Ollama to analyze mission conditions and provide recommendations.

I also developed a resource forecasting feature that predicts how oxygen, water, food, and power could change over the next 5, 10, or 20 Martian days.

This helps demonstrate how astronauts could identify potential shortages before they become serious problems.

Connecting Software with Hardware

I wanted my project to go beyond a website, so I connected an ESP32 microcontroller with an OLED display and buzzer.

The ESP32 receives mission information from the backend through Wi-Fi.

The OLED displays live resource levels and mission status. When the system detects a critical emergency, the buzzer provides an audible warning.

This demonstrates how digital monitoring and physical alert systems can work together.

Technologies I Used

  • React and Vite for the interactive dashboard
  • Node.js and Express for the backend
  • Ollama with Llama 3.2 for AI recommendations
  • ESP32 for hardware integration
  • OLED display for real-time mission information
  • Buzzer for emergency alerts
  • Resource forecasting and simulation logic for predicting shortages

What I Learned and My Future Plans

Building MARS-SAFE Explorers helped me understand how software, AI, and electronics can be connected into one working system.

One of the most interesting parts was seeing an emergency triggered on my website appear on the ESP32 OLED display.

This project is currently a simulation and working prototype, not a system ready for actual space missions.

In the future, I would like to add physical environmental sensors, improve the AI recommendations, and develop more automated emergency responses.

My goal is to continue exploring how technology could support safer and more independent human exploration of Mars.
